title: Semantics and Pragmatics
overview: Meaning involves conventional linguistic content, contextual interpretation and communicative action. Begin with words, relations and theories, then examine inference, deixis and speech acts. Politeness, conversation analysis and textual organisation connect these ideas to real interaction.
journey: Understand conventional content: sense, reference, propositions and lexical relations.
Compare explanations: structural, cognitive, behavioural, truth-conditional and generative approaches.
Interpret use: context, implicature, deixis, speech acts and face.
Read interaction and text: sequences, repair, cohesion and coherence.

topics.title: Meaning and its difficulties
topics.core: Linguistic meaning concerns what expressions contribute to interpretation and communication.
topics.explanation: Meaning can refer to conventional content, contextual reference or a speaker's intended message. Ambiguity, context and differing analytical goals make one universal definition difficult.
topics.example: Teaching example: It's cold can describe temperature and, in context, prompt someone to close a window.
topics.confusion: Meaning is not identical to one person's private association with a word.

keyPoints: Linguistic meaning concerns what expressions contribute to interpretation and communication.
Meaning is not identical to one person's private association with a word.

questions.prompt: Why is looking up every word insufficient to understand an utterance?
questions.shortAnswer: Dictionary meanings do not determine every referent, context or communicative intention.
questions.answer: Dictionary meanings do not determine every referent, context or communicative intention. A hearer also interprets how the words are being used in the situation.
keyPoints: Dictionary meanings do not determine every referent, context or communicative intention.
A hearer also interprets how the words are being used in the situation.

topics.title: Levels of meaning
topics.core: Expression meaning concerns conventional content, utterance meaning its contextual use, and communicative meaning the message conveyed.
topics.explanation: The levels distinguish a language expression from a particular use and the speaker's intended contribution.
topics.example: Teaching example: It's late has conventional content, a contextual time reference and possibly an intended request to leave.
topics.confusion: These levels interact; they are analytical distinctions rather than three unrelated messages.

questions.prompt: How can 'The door is open' convey more than its literal description?
questions.shortAnswer: In context it may invite entry or request closure.
questions.answer: In context it may invite entry or request closure. The sentence content describes a state, while communicative interpretation adds the relevant intended action.
keyPoints: In context it may invite entry or request closure.

topics.title: Descriptive, social and expressive meaning
topics.core: Descriptive meaning represents situations; social meaning indexes social relationships; expressive meaning conveys attitudes or feelings.
topics.explanation: An expression can contribute more than one dimension. The guide supplies this three-part account rather than a complete inventory of every textbook taxonomy.
topics.example: Teaching example: A formal title indexes a social relation; an insulting word can add negative attitude.
topics.confusion: An expression's emotional associations are not automatically part of its descriptive truth conditions.

questions.shortAnswer: One may use a formal title and another an intimate nickname.
questions.answer: One may use a formal title and another an intimate nickname. Their reference can coincide while they position the speaker's relationship differently.

topics.title: Sense
topics.core: Sense is the semantic content through which an expression is understood, distinct from a particular referent.
topics.explanation: Expressions can share a referent while presenting it differently. The guide gives limited technical coverage of sense.
topics.example: Teaching example: Morning star and evening star can identify Venus through different descriptions.
topics.confusion: A sense is not simply the object referred to.

questions.prompt: Why can 'morning star' and 'evening star' differ in sense while sharing reference?
questions.shortAnswer: They present the object through different descriptive modes.
questions.answer: They present the object through different descriptive modes. In the relevant astronomical interpretation both refer to Venus, but they do not convey the same descriptive information.
keyPoints: They present the object through different descriptive modes.

topics.title: Reference and denotation
topics.core: Reference identifies an entity in use; denotation concerns what an expression conventionally applies to.
topics.explanation: A common noun can denote a category, while a speaker uses a noun phrase to identify a particular member.
topics.example: Teaching example: Cat applies to cats generally; that cat can refer to a particular animal in context.
topics.confusion: Reference needs not be fixed solely by dictionary meaning.

keyPoints: Reference identifies an entity in use; denotation concerns what an expression conventionally applies to.

questions.prompt: What information is needed to identify the referent of 'that book'?
questions.shortAnswer: The expression's meaning provides instructions, but the situation, gesture or previous discourse helps identify which particular book the speaker intends.

topics.title: Propositions
topics.core: A proposition is the content that can be asserted, denied or evaluated for truth.
topics.explanation: Different sentence forms can be related to the same situation content, while questions need not assert it.
topics.example: Teaching example: The door is open and Is the door open? concern the same possible state.
topics.confusion: A proposition is not simply the sequence of words in a sentence.

questions.prompt: Explain propositions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A proposition is the content that can be asserted, denied or evaluated for truth.

questions.prompt: Can two differently worded sentences express the same proposition?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes, in an appropriate context they can convey the same truth-evaluable content.
questions.answer: Yes, in an appropriate context they can convey the same truth-evaluable content. Wording, sentence form and propositional content should be distinguished.

topics.title: Ambiguity, homonymy and polysemy
topics.core: Ambiguity allows distinct readings; homonymy involves unrelated lexical meanings, while polysemy involves related meanings.
topics.explanation: Lexical ambiguity can come from homonymy or polysemy; structural ambiguity comes from alternative grammatical organisation.
topics.example: Teaching example: Bank can mean a financial institution or a river edge; head has several related uses.
topics.confusion: Relatedness is sometimes debatable; contextual variation does not always establish a stored lexical sense.

topics.title: Vagueness
topics.core: Vagueness concerns unclear boundaries within a reading rather than several distinct readings.
topics.explanation: A vague term can have borderline cases even when its intended sense is understood.
topics.example: Teaching example: Tall has no single context-free height boundary.
topics.confusion: A vague word need not have two separate dictionary senses.

questions.shortAnswer: The issue is the boundary of one gradable meaning, not choosing between distinct unrelated readings.
questions.answer: The issue is the boundary of one gradable meaning, not choosing between distinct unrelated readings. The relevant standard can vary with context.

topics.title: Lexical and grammatical meaning
topics.core: Lexical meaning is associated with vocabulary items; grammatical meaning is contributed by forms and constructions.
topics.explanation: Inflections, function words and word order can express number, tense or participant relations.
topics.example: Teaching example: Dog contributes lexical content while plural -s adds grammatical number.
topics.confusion: Grammatical meaning is not empty or less meaningful than lexical content.

questions.prompt: What meaning changes between 'the dog chased the cat' and 'the cat chased the dog'?
questions.shortAnswer: The lexical items remain largely the same, but word order changes the participant roles expressed by the construction, producing different situation meanings.

topics.title: Componential analysis
topics.core: Componential analysis represents word meanings through combinations of semantic features.
topics.explanation: It is useful for explicit contrasts within a lexical set, but some meanings resist a simple feature checklist.
topics.example: Teaching example: A simplified comparison can distinguish adult versus non-adult and male versus female terms.
topics.confusion: A convenient feature analysis is a model, not proof that all meaning consists of binary features.

questions.prompt: Explain componential analysis briefly.

questions.shortAnswer: Some categories have vague boundaries, context-sensitive use or typicality effects.

topics.title: Semantic roles
topics.core: Semantic roles describe how participants relate to an event, such as agent, theme or patient.
topics.explanation: An agent typically initiates an action; a patient is affected; a theme is involved or moved. Role inventories differ across frameworks.
topics.example: Teaching example: In The child broke the cup, child is agent and cup is patient.
topics.confusion: Semantic roles do not equal grammatical functions: a subject need not be an agent.

questions.prompt: In 'The cup was broken by the child', is the subject the agent?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. The cup is the grammatical subject but the affected patient. The child remains the agent in the passive construction.

topics.title: Synonymy and near-synonymy
topics.core: Synonymy concerns sameness or close similarity of meaning between expressions.
topics.explanation: Near synonyms can differ in register, distribution, connotation or collocation, so complete interchangeability is unusual.
topics.example: Teaching example: Begin and commence overlap, but commence is typically more formal.
topics.confusion: Sharing a referent does not automatically make two expressions synonyms.

topics.title: Hyponymy and meronymy
topics.core: Hyponymy is a kind-of relation; meronymy is a part-of relation.
topics.explanation: These organise vocabulary in different ways and should be identified by the relevant conceptual link.
topics.example: Teaching example: Rose is a kind of flower; petal is part of a flower.
topics.confusion: A part is not necessarily a subtype of its whole.

topics.title: Antonymy and complementarity
topics.core: Antonymy concerns oppositeness; complementary terms divide a relevant domain into mutually exclusive alternatives.
topics.explanation: Gradable opposites permit degrees and often a middle range. Complementarity depends on the domain and interpretation.
topics.example: Teaching example: Hot and cold allow warm; alive and dead can be complementary in an ordinary specified context.
topics.confusion: Not hot does not normally entail cold.

topics.title: Structural theories of meaning
topics.core: Structural approaches explain meanings through relations within a language system.
topics.explanation: Contrast and combination help determine a lexical item's place in a semantic network.
topics.example: Teaching example: Hot is partly understood through relations with warm, cool and cold.
topics.confusion: A word's meaning is not explained only by pointing to an external object.

topics.title: Behaviourist approaches to meaning
topics.core: Behaviourist approaches seek to explain verbal meaning through observable conditions and responses.
topics.explanation: Bloomfield connected utterances with the practical situations preceding and following speech. This offers a different explanatory emphasis from mental concepts.
topics.example: Teaching example: A request is considered in relation to its circumstances and the listener's practical response.
topics.confusion: A stimulus–response sketch does not provide a complete analysis of every abstract or novel meaning.

topics.title: Cognitive semantics
topics.core: Cognitive approaches connect meaning with conceptualisation and categorisation.
topics.explanation: Concepts, prototypes and background knowledge help explain interpretation, while the guide distinguishes conventional meaning from richer personal knowledge.
topics.example: Teaching example: A robin can seem more typical of BIRD than a penguin.
topics.confusion: Typicality is not identical to membership: a less typical penguin is still fully a bird.

topics.title: Truth-conditional semantics
topics.core: A truth-conditional account asks what must hold for a statement to be true.
topics.explanation: Specify the reading and contextual reference before evaluating its truth. Truth conditions differ from whether we currently know the statement is true.
topics.example: Teaching example: The window is open is true only if the relevant window is open in the relevant situation.
topics.confusion: A statement can have clear truth conditions even when its truth is unknown.

topics.title: Generative semantics
topics.core: Historical generative semantics explored a close derivational relationship between semantic representations and sentence structure.
topics.explanation: It developed within debates about transformational grammar, with scholars including Lakoff, McCawley, Postal and Ross. The syllabus's broad label should be distinguished from other generative approaches.
topics.example: Teaching example: An analysis may decompose a lexical predicate into abstract semantic components used in deriving a sentence.
topics.confusion: Generative semantics, Chomskyan grammar and the Generative Lexicon are not interchangeable labels.

topics.title: Metaphor
topics.core: Metaphor uses a source domain to structure or describe a different target domain through selected similarities.
topics.explanation: The comparison transfers relevant features rather than asserting literal identity.

topics.core: A sentence is an abstract linguistic form; an utterance is a particular instance of language use.
topics.explanation: The same sentence can be uttered by different people at different times with different references or intentions.
topics.example: Teaching example: I am here refers differently when spoken by two people in different places.
topics.confusion: An utterance can be a fragment rather than a complete sentence.

questions.prompt: Can 'Coffee?' count as an utterance even though it is not a full sentence?

topics.title: Context
topics.core: Context includes linguistic surroundings, the situation, participants and relevant background assumptions.
topics.explanation: It helps resolve reference, ambiguity and intended actions. Shared knowledge may be incomplete and open to correction.
topics.example: Teaching example: She's ready requires a relevant person and activity to interpret she and ready.
topics.confusion: Context is not only the preceding sentence.

topics.title: Entailment
topics.core: Entailment is a relation in which one proposition's truth guarantees another's, under a fixed interpretation.
topics.explanation: It is a semantic consequence rather than merely a likely inference.
topics.example: Teaching example: Amina owns a poodle entails Amina owns a dog under the relevant ordinary meanings.
topics.confusion: A plausible consequence is not necessarily an entailment.

questions.prompt: Does 'Amina owns a dog' entail 'Amina owns a poodle'?

topics.title: Presupposition and triggers
topics.core: A presupposition is background information treated as already accepted or required for an utterance.
topics.explanation: Definite expressions, factive verbs and change-of-state expressions can trigger presuppositions. Projection through negation is a useful diagnostic, with contextual qualifications.
topics.example: Teaching example: She stopped smoking normally presupposes that she previously smoked.
topics.confusion: Presuppositions can be challenged, accommodated or blocked in context.

questions.prompt: How does 'She did not stop smoking' help distinguish presupposition from entailment?

topics.title: Conventional and conversational implicature
topics.core: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations.
topics.explanation: Conversational implicatures can often be cancelled or changed by context. A generalized inference needs less special context than a particularized one.
topics.example: Teaching example: Some passed may suggest not all, yet 'in fact, all did' can cancel that inference.
topics.confusion: Conversational implicature is not a strict logical entailment.

topics.title: Cooperation and conversational maxims
topics.core: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose.
topics.explanation: The maxims concern Quality, Quantity, Relation and Manner: truthfulness, informativeness, relevance and clarity.
topics.example: Teaching example: A concise relevant answer supports the current task.
topics.confusion: Cooperation is a framework for interpreting conversation, not a rule requiring social agreement.

topics.title: Flouting and violating maxims
topics.core: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation.
topics.explanation: A hearer may infer irony or an indirect message when the apparent mismatch is openly recognisable.

topics.confusion: A maxim departure is not automatically deliberate or interpretable as one fixed message.

topics.title: Deixis and the deictic centre
topics.core: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates.
topics.explanation: The ordinary centre is speaker, here and now. Some uses are anaphoric rather than deictic, depending on how a referent is identified.
topics.example: Teaching example: I will meet you here tomorrow needs a speaker, addressee, location and date.
topics.confusion: A form such as that can have deictic or anaphoric uses.

topics.title: Deictic projection
topics.core: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now.
topics.explanation: A narrative or represented viewpoint can organise deictic expressions around another participant, time or location.
topics.example: Teaching example: A narrator may use now from a character's represented moment.

topics.title: Types of deixis
topics.core: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis.
topics.explanation: Person concerns participant roles, place and time locate events, discourse points within communication and social deixis encodes relationships.

topics.title: Honorifics
topics.core: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality.
topics.explanation: They can concern the addressee or a person being referred to; their precise forms and meanings are language-specific.

topics.title: Performatives and constatives
topics.core: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation.
topics.explanation: Austin's initial distinction motivated a wider theory in which ordinary assertions are also actions.

topics.title: Felicity conditions
topics.core: Felicity conditions are the contextual and procedural requirements for a speech act to be appropriate or successfully performed.

topics.title: Searle's speech-act categories

questions.shortAnswer: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker.
questions.answer: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker. A first pair part makes a limited range of second actions relevant, such as a greeting and return greeting.
keyPoints: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker.
Adjacency is an organisational relation, not a claim that the turns must always be physically next to each other.

questions.prompt: Can an adjacency pair remain connected when another exchange intervenes?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. An insertion sequence can occur between its first and second parts while the original response remains conditionally relevant.
keyPoints: Yes.
An insertion sequence can occur between its first and second parts while the original response remains conditionally relevant.

topics.title: The semantics–pragmatics interface
topics.core: Semantics and pragmatics distinguish conventional linguistic contributions from context-sensitive use and inference, while interacting in interpretation.
topics.explanation: Deictic reference and implied messages show why the boundary is analytically useful but theoretically debated.
topics.example: Teaching example: The conventional meaning of I identifies a speaker role; context determines its referent.
topics.confusion: Semantics is not wholly unrelated to context, and pragmatics is not unrestricted guesswork.

questions.prompt: Why is 'semantics is completely context-free' an oversimplification?
questions.shortAnswer: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule.
questions.answer: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule. Theories differ on where to locate particular contextual contributions.

topics.title: Cohesion
topics.core: Cohesion consists of identifiable linguistic ties connecting parts of a text.
topics.explanation: Reference, substitution, ellipsis, lexical relations and conjunction can link clauses or turns.
topics.example: Teaching example: A student arrived. She sat down uses an anaphoric reference tie.
topics.confusion: Cohesive devices alone do not guarantee a sensible overall message.

questions.prompt: Can a passage contain many connectives yet remain incoherent?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Explicit ties can link sentences formally while their ideas fail to make sense together. Coherence needs an interpretable relationship, not only markers.
keyPoints: Yes.
Explicit ties can link sentences formally while their ideas fail to make sense together.
Coherence needs an interpretable relationship, not only markers.

topics.title: Reference ties
topics.core: Reference ties connect an expression with an entity interpreted through text or situation.
topics.explanation: Anaphora points back; cataphora points forward. Endophoric reference is text-internal, while exophoric reference depends on the situation.
topics.example: Teaching example: When she entered, Amina smiled can use a following name to resolve she.
topics.confusion: Exophoric reference may support interpretation without forming a text-internal tie.

questions.prompt: Explain reference ties briefly.

questions.prompt: How do anaphora and deixis differ?
questions.shortAnswer: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates.
questions.answer: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates. Some expressions can serve either role depending on use.
keyPoints: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates.
Some expressions can serve either role depending on use.

topics.title: Substitution and ellipsis
topics.core: Substitution replaces material with a grammatical substitute; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken.
topics.explanation: They can involve nominal, verbal or clausal material, depending on the construction.
topics.example: Teaching example: I need a pen. Have you got one? substitutes one; Have you finished? Yes, I have leaves finished understood.
topics.confusion: A pronoun's reference relation is not automatically the same as grammatical substitution.

questions.prompt: What is omitted in 'Has she finished the essay? Yes, she has'?
questions.shortAnswer: The material finished the essay is recoverable from the question.
questions.answer: The material finished the essay is recoverable from the question. The auxiliary remains while the repeated verbal content is elided.

topics.title: Lexical cohesion
topics.core: Lexical cohesion connects a text through vocabulary relations and associations.
topics.explanation: Reiteration can use repetition, near synonyms, superordinates or general words. Associated vocabulary can also establish links.
topics.example: Teaching example: A sparrow landed. The bird rested uses a superordinate to maintain the referent.
topics.confusion: Related words need not be interchangeable synonyms.

questions.prompt: Why does 'The oven was hot. Its heat warmed the kitchen' show lexical cohesion?
questions.shortAnswer: Hot and heat are related lexical choices that maintain the temperature theme and connect the two descriptions.
questions.answer: Hot and heat are related lexical choices that maintain the temperature theme and connect the two descriptions.

topics.title: Conjunction in discourse
topics.core: Conjunction marks relations such as addition, contrast, cause or sequence between discourse parts.
topics.explanation: Interpret the connection signalled by and, however, therefore or then in its actual context.
topics.example: Teaching example: It rained. Therefore, the match stopped presents the second event as a result.
topics.confusion: A temporal sequence does not by itself establish causation.

questions.prompt: Why do then and therefore suggest different relations?
questions.shortAnswer: Then primarily orders events in time, while therefore presents a consequence or inference.
questions.answer: Then primarily orders events in time, while therefore presents a consequence or inference. A sequence alone need not imply that one event caused the next.
keyPoints: Then primarily orders events in time, while therefore presents a consequence or inference.
A sequence alone need not imply that one event caused the next.

topics.title: Coherence
topics.core: Coherence is the meaningful connectedness that makes discourse interpretable as a whole.
topics.explanation: Hearers use context, shared knowledge and inference to connect ideas, including brief exchanges with few overt ties.
topics.example: Teaching example: A: A walk? B: My ankle. can refuse when an injury is shared knowledge.
topics.confusion: Coherence is not identical to grammatical correctness or visible cohesion.

questions.prompt: How can 'A walk?'—'My ankle' be coherent without an explicit refusal?
questions.shortAnswer: Shared knowledge of an ankle injury can make the second fragment a relevant reason for declining.
questions.answer: Shared knowledge of an ankle injury can make the second fragment a relevant reason for declining. The hearer supplies the context-supported connection.
